body_content:
Comparative and Superlative Adjectives

Practice Comparative Adjectives.

Superlative adjectives

Use the superlative to compare one thing with the whole group: add -est to short adjectives (the fastest) or use the most with longer ones (the most expensive). Watch for irregulars: good → the best, bad → the worst.

title: Future: going to / will

revision.summary: Practice Future: going to.
revision.note: Extended this pass to cover a previously PARTIAL syllabus item (see A2_CURRICULUM_ISSUES.md issue F), per Agent 6 default in the absence of an explicit human ruling on issue F specifically — flagged for review.

body_content:
Future: going to / will

Practice Future: going to.

Going further: will

Use will for predictions based on opinion (I think it will rain) and for decisions made at the moment of speaking (I'll answer that). Use going to for plans and predictions based on present evidence (Look at those clouds — it's going to rain).

Say it: going to

In fast speech going to often becomes gonna /ˈɡʌnə/. I'm going to call him = "I'm gonna call him". Use gonna in speech, but write going to.

Where accents differ

UKI'm going to have a rest.
I'll have a lie-down.
USI'm going to take a rest.
I'll take a nap.
Say it: "I'm gonna study tonight. We're gonna travel in July."

title: Countable/Uncountable

revision.summary: Practice Countable/Uncountable.
revision.note: Off-syllabus lesson (not in CURRICULUM_SOURCE.md's A2 list); kept per human decision at the approval gate and revised here with additional depth rather than removed.

body_content:
Countable/Uncountable

Practice Countable/Uncountable.

Going further

Some nouns are countable in some languages but uncountable in English (advice, information, furniture, luggage). Use 'a piece of', 'a bit of' or 'some' with these instead of a plural form.

More examples

  • She gave me some useful advice.
  • I need a few pieces of information.
  • We don't have much furniture yet.

revision.summary: Practice Adverbs of Frequency.

body_content:
Adverbs of Frequency and Manner

Practice Adverbs of Frequency.

Adverbs of manner

Adverbs of manner describe how an action happens and usually end in -ly (quickly, carefully, badly). They normally go after the verb (or object): She spoke quietly. Note: good → well, not goodly.

title: Modal: should

revision.summary: Practice Modal: should.
revision.note: Off-syllabus lesson (not in CURRICULUM_SOURCE.md's A2 list); kept per human decision at the approval gate and revised here with additional depth rather than removed.

body_content:
Modal: should

Practice Modal: should.

Going further

'Should' gives advice or an opinion, and is weaker than 'must' (obligation) or 'have to' (necessity). Use 'shouldn't' for advice against doing something, and 'should + have + past participle' to talk about a past mistake (You should have called me).

More examples

  • You should have called me yesterday.
  • I don't think you should say that.
  • Should I bring anything to the party?

Say it: should

In should the letter l is silent: /ʃʊd/. In advice, stress the main verb: You should REST. Shouldn't /ˈʃʊdnt/ has two syllables.

Say it: "You should see a doctor. You shouldn't work today."

title: Present Simple

revision.summary:
Use the present simple for facts, habits and routines. The present simple describes things that are generally
true or that happen regularly. Add -s/-es for he/she/it. Use don't/
doesn't for negatives and questions.

body_content:
Present Simple

Use the present simple for facts, habits and routines. The present simple describes things that are generally true or that happen regularly. Add -s/-es for he/she/it. Use don't/ doesn't for negatives and questions.

Going further at A2

This builds on A1 basics with more complex sentences, mixed time expressions, and less predictable irregular forms, plus a different practice style (transformation and error-correction rather than simple gap-fill) so learners who already met this at A1 are stretched, not just reminded.

Examples

  • She works in a hospital.
  • We don't eat meat.
  • Does he live near here?
  • The shop opens at nine.

Key terms

Present Simple

title: Past Simple

revision.summary:
Talk about finished actions and events in the past. Regular verbs add -ed; many common verbs are
irregular. Use didn't for negatives and did for questions (base verb
after did/didn't).
examples: I visited my grandparents last weekend.
She went to Paris in June.

body_content:
Past Simple

Talk about finished actions and events in the past. Regular verbs add -ed; many common verbs are irregular. Use didn't for negatives and did for questions (base verb after did/didn't).

Going further at A2

This builds on A1 basics with more complex sentences, mixed time expressions, and less predictable irregular forms, plus a different practice style (transformation and error-correction rather than simple gap-fill) so learners who already met this at A1 are stretched, not just reminded.

Examples

  • I visited my grandparents last weekend.
  • She went to Paris in June.
  • We didn't watch the film.
  • Did you call him yesterday?

Key terms

Past Simple

Say it: irregular past forms

Some irregular verbs sound the same as other words: read /red/ (past) but /riːd/ (present); went, saw /sɔː/, bought /bɔːt/. Say the vowel clearly.

Where accents differ

UKgot (past of get)
learnt / learned
USgotten (past participle of get)
learned
Say it: "I read that book. I bought a coat. We went home."

title: Reflexive Pronouns

revision.summary:
Use reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself, himself,
herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves) correctly. Use a reflexive pronoun when the subject and object of
a verb are the same person or thing.
examples: They enjoyed themselves at the party.
Be careful — you might hurt yourself.

body_content:
Reflexive Pronouns

Use reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves) correctly. Use a reflexive pronoun when the subject and object of a verb are the same person or thing.

Examples

  • I cut myself while cooking.
  • She taught herself Spanish.
  • They enjoyed themselves at the party.
  • Be careful — you might hurt yourself.

Key terms

Reflexive Pronouns

title: So / Such

revision.summary:
Use so and such to add emphasis to adjectives and nouns. Use "so" directly before an adjective or adverb ("so
tired"). Use "such" before a noun, or an adjective + noun ("such a
long day").

body_content:
So / Such

Use so and such to add emphasis to adjectives and nouns. Use "so" directly before an adjective or adverb ("so tired"). Use "such" before a noun, or an adjective + noun ("such a long day").

Examples

  • The film was so boring.
  • It's such a beautiful city.
  • She speaks so quickly.
  • They are such good friends.

Key terms

So / Such

title: Have to / Need to (Obligation)

revision.summary:
Express obligation and necessity. "Have to" and "need to" both show something is
necessary. Use don't have to / don't need to for "not necessary"
(different meaning from "must not").
examples: I have to finish this report today.
You don't need to bring anything.
Does she have to work on Saturdays?

body_content:
Have to / Need to (Obligation)

Express obligation and necessity. "Have to" and "need to" both show something is necessary. Use don't have to / don't need to for "not necessary" (different meaning from "must not").

Examples

  • I have to finish this report today.
  • You don't need to bring anything.
  • Does she have to work on Saturdays?
  • We need to leave before 8am.

Key terms

Have to / Need to (Obligation)

Say it: have to

Have to is usually pronounced /ˈhæftə/ and has to /ˈhæstə/. Stress the main verb: I have to GO. Don't have to means it is not necessary.

Say it: "I have to work today. She has to study."

title: When / While

revision.summary:
Use when and while to connect two actions in time. "While" is often used with a longer, ongoing action
(often past continuous); "when" often introduces a shorter action that
interrupts or follows.
examples: While I was cooking, the phone rang.
When she arrived, we started the meeting.
He read a book while he waited.
When it rains, I take an umbrella.

body_content:
When / While

Use when and while to connect two actions in time. "While" is often used with a longer, ongoing action (often past continuous); "when" often introduces a shorter action that interrupts or follows.

Examples

  • While I was cooking, the phone rang.
  • When she arrived, we started the meeting.
  • He read a book while he waited.
  • When it rains, I take an umbrella.

Key terms

When / While

title: Must / Might for Deductions

revision.summary:
Make logical deductions about the present. Use "must" when you're almost certain something is
true; use "might" (or "may"/"could") when it's only possible.
examples: The lights are off — they must be out.
She might be at work; I'm not sure.
He must be tired after that trip.

body_content:
Must / Might for Deductions

Make logical deductions about the present. Use "must" when you're almost certain something is true; use "might" (or "may"/"could") when it's only possible.

Examples

  • The lights are off — they must be out.
  • She might be at work; I'm not sure.
  • He must be tired after that trip.
  • It might rain later.

Key terms

Must / Might for Deductions

Listen for: must and might

In deductions the modal is short and the main idea is stressed: He must be TIRED. She might be at HOME. Listen for must /mʌst/ (very sure) and might /maɪt/ (not sure).

Listen: is the speaker sure (must) or not sure (might)?

title: As Soon As

revision.summary:
Use "as soon as" to talk about one action happening
immediately after another. "As soon as" introduces a time clause; the main clause
often uses will/going to for a future result.
examples: I'll call you as soon as I land.
As soon as she gets home, she checks her email.
We'll start as soon as everyone arrives.
He left as soon as the meeting ended.

body_content:
As Soon As

Use "as soon as" to talk about one action happening immediately after another. "As soon as" introduces a time clause; the main clause often uses will/going to for a future result.

Examples

title: Be Able To / Good At

revision.summary:
Talk about ability and skill. "Be able to" describes ability (can be used in more
tenses than "can"); "good at" + noun/gerund describes skill level.
examples: I wasn't able to finish on time.
Will you be able to come tomorrow?
He's good at explaining things clearly.

body_content:
Be Able To / Good At

Talk about ability and skill. "Be able to" describes ability (can be used in more tenses than "can"); "good at" + noun/gerund describes skill level.

Examples

  • I wasn't able to finish on time.

title: Although / However

revision.summary:
Show contrast between two ideas. "Although" joins two clauses in one sentence.
"However" usually starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma.
examples: Although it was raining, we went for a walk.
The trip was long. However, it was worth it.
She passed the test although she didn't study much.
He's friendly. However, he's also very shy.

body_content:
Although / However

Show contrast between two ideas. "Although" joins two clauses in one sentence. "However" usually starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma.

Examples

  • Although it was raining, we went for a walk.
  • The trip was long. However, it was worth it.
  • She passed the test although she didn't study much.
  • He's friendly. However, he's also very shy.

Key terms

Although / However

title: Used To

revision.summary:
Talk about past habits and states that are no longer
true. "Used to" + base verb describes a repeated past action
or state that has changed. Negative: didn't use to.
examples: I used to live in Rome.
She didn't use to like coffee.
Did you use to play an instrument?
We used to walk to school every day.

body_content:
Used To

Talk about past habits and states that are no longer true. "Used to" + base verb describes a repeated past action or state that has changed. Negative: didn't use to.

Examples

  • I used to live in Rome.
  • She didn't use to like coffee.
  • Did you use to play an instrument?
  • We used to walk to school every day.

Key terms

Used To

Say it: used to

Used to is pronounced /ˈjuːstə/: the d is not heard. Compare I used to play (past habit) with I'm used to it (I am accustomed).

Say it: "I used to live in a village. We used to play football."

title: Relative Clauses

revision.summary:
Add extra information about a noun using who, which,
that, where. "Who" for people, "which" for things, "that" for
either (informal), "where" for places.
examples: The woman who called you is my sister.
This is the book that I told you about.
We visited the town where I was born.
The car, which is new, is parked outside.

body_content:
Relative Clauses

Add extra information about a noun using who, which, that, where. "Who" for people, "which" for things, "that" for either (informal), "where" for places.

Examples

Predict future outcomes in conversation.

Examples

  • I bet...
  • I reckon...
  • It's likely to...
  • I doubt it'll...

Key terms

I bet..., I reckon..., It's likely to..., I doubt it'll...

title: Offering and Suggesting

revision.summary: Offer help or suggest an activity politely.

body_content:
Offering and Suggesting

Offer help or suggest an activity politely.

Examples

  • Shall I...?
  • Why don't we...?
  • How about...?
  • Would you like me to...?

Key terms

Shall I...?, Why don't we...?, How about...?, Would you like me to...?

Say it: offers and suggestions

Offers and suggestions sound friendly with a rising voice: Shall I help you? ↗ Why don't we go out? ↗ A flat voice can sound unfriendly.

Say it: "Would you like some tea? Let's go to the park."

title: Talking About Obligation

revision.summary: Express what is necessary or required in conversation.

body_content:
Talking About Obligation

Express what is necessary or required in conversation.

Examples

  • I have to...
  • I'm supposed to...
  • It's compulsory to...
  • You don't have to
  • but...

Key terms

I have to..., I'm supposed to..., It's compulsory to..., You don't have to

title: Requesting

revision.summary: Make polite requests.
examples: I was wondering if you could...
key_terms: I was wondering if you could...

body_content:
Requesting

Make polite requests.

Examples

  • Could you...?
  • Would you mind...?
  • Do you think you could...?
  • I was wondering if you could...

Key terms

Could you...?, Would you mind...?, Do you think you could...?, I was wondering if you could...

Say it: polite requests

Use a gentle rise and clear please: Could you open the window, please? ↗ Say could you quickly /kʊdʒə/ and keep the request sound polite, not sharp.

Say it: "Could you help me, please? Can I use your pen?"

title: Sounds: /ɪ/ and /iː/

revision.summary: Hear and say the short vowel /ɪ/ and the long vowel /iː/ so that pairs like ship / sheep and live / leave are clear.

body_content:
Sounds: /ɪ/ and /iː/

Many learners use one sound for both vowels. In English the difference changes the word, so it matters. In this lesson you practise a short, relaxed /ɪ/ and a longer, tighter /iː/.

1. Two different sounds

  • /ɪ/ is short. Your mouth is relaxed and a little open: ship, it, sit, live, bit.
  • /iː/ is long. Smile a little and hold the sound: sheep, eat, seat, leave, beat.

2. Minimal pairs

A minimal pair is two words that differ by one sound. Say each pair slowly, then quickly: ship / sheep, sit / seat, live / leave, bit / beat, fill / feel.

Check: Please sit down and Please seat down are different. Only the first is correct.

3. Spelling helps a little

ee and ea often make /iː/ (see, meat). The letter i between consonants is often /ɪ/ (big, this). There are exceptions, so always learn the sound with the word.

4. Where accents differ

The two vowels exist in both accents. Some words change:

UKbeen = /biːn/ (long vowel)
either = /ˈaɪðə/ (or /ˈiːðə/)
ski = /skiː/
USbeen = /bɪn/ (short vowel)
either = /ˈiːðər/ (or /ˈaɪðər/)
ski = /skiː/

Both are correct. Learn one accent first and recognise the other.

Practice tip: record yourself saying "ship, sheep, sit, seat" and listen for a clear length difference.

title: Past Endings: -ed

revision.summary: Learn the three sounds of the -ed ending (/t/, /d/, /ɪd/) in regular past verbs and adjectives, and decide which one to use from the last sound of the verb.

body_content:
Past Endings: -ed

Regular past verbs end in -ed, but you do not always say "ed". The ending has three sounds, and the right one depends on the last sound of the verb.

1. The three sounds

  • /t/ after /p/, /k/, /f/, /s/, /ʃ/, /tʃ/: stopped, worked, laughed, missed, washed, watched.
  • /d/ after other sounds (vowels and /b/, /g/, /l/, /m/, /n/, /v/): played, opened, lived, called, cleaned.
  • /ɪd/ after /t/ and /d/: wanted, needed, started, decided. This ending adds a syllable.

2. Count the syllables

Walked has one syllable. Wanted has two. If you say "walk-ed", listeners may be confused. Only /t/ and /d/ verbs get the extra syllable.

3. Practise in sentences

Yesterday I worked /t/, played /d/ and waited /ɪd/ for the bus.

4. Where accents differ

The three sounds are the same in both accents. A few verbs have a different past form or spelling:

UKlearnt or learned
spelt or spelled
dreamt or dreamed
USlearned (usual form)
spelled (usual form)
dreamed (usual form)
Practice tip: say the base verb, then the -ed form, and clap once for each syllable.

title: Weak Forms: to and can

revision.summary: Learn why small words like to and can are usually weak (/tə/, /kən/) and when they are strong, so that natural speech becomes easier to say and understand.
examples: I want to go /aɪ wɒnt tə ɡəʊ/

body_content:
Weak Forms: to and can

In natural speech, small grammar words are short and quiet. The vowel becomes a weak sound called schwa /ə/. Content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) are strong and clear.

1. The word to

Before a verb, to is weak: /tə/. "I want to go" sounds like "I wanna go" (only in informal speech). Say: want to, need to, have to, going to.

2. The word can

In a positive sentence can is weak: /kən/. "I can swim" = /aɪ kən swɪm/. The verb swim gets the stress.

In a short answer, can is strong: Yes, I can /kæn/.

3. Can or can't?

The negative can't is always strong and the vowel is longer. Listen for the stress on the verb and the length of the vowel:

  • I can swim = short, weak can.
  • I can't swim = clear, strong can't.

4. Where accents differ

Weak forms are used in both accents. The negative sounds different:

UKcan't = /kɑːnt/ (long vowel)
can weak = /kən/
UScan't = /kænt/ (short vowel)
can weak = /kən/
In US speech can't is often heard as /kæn/ with a very short t
Practice tip: say a sentence with "can" in two ways: "I can swim" and "Yes, I can". Feel the different vowel.

title: Listening: Daily Routines

revision.summary: Practise listening to people talk about their daily routines, catching times, frequency words and activities, with UK and US differences in times and dates.
examples: I get up at half past six.
She usually has lunch at one.

body_content:
Listening: Daily Routines

When people describe their day, you hear the same things: a time, an activity and a frequency word (always, usually, sometimes, never). Read each script aloud, then cover it and answer from memory.

1. Listening strategy

  • Before: decide what to listen for (times, activities).
  • During: catch stressed words. They carry the meaning.
  • After: check with the script.

2. Script 1: a morning

I get up at half past six. I have a shower and eat breakfast at seven. I usually leave home at quarter to eight, and I never miss the bus.

Times: 6:30, 7:00, 7:45. Frequency words: usually, never.

3. Script 2: a dialogue

A: What time do you finish work?
B: At five, but on Fridays I finish at three.
A: And do you always cook dinner?
B: No, sometimes we order pizza.

Key details: 5:00, Fridays at 3:00, sometimes.

4. Frequency words on a scale

always (100%) > usually > often > sometimes > rarely > never (0%). These words are stressed, so they are easy to hear.

5. Where UK and US differ

UKhalf past six = 6:30
quarter past seven = 7:15
at the weekend
date: 29/9 (day/month)
USsix thirty (or half past six) = 6:30
a quarter after seven = 7:15
on the weekend
date: 9/29 (month/day)
Practice tip: write your own day in five sentences with times, then read it to a friend who writes down the times only.

title: Listening: Shopping

revision.summary: Practise listening to shopping conversations, catching prices, sizes, colours and quantities, with UK and US vocabulary differences.
examples: How much is this jumper? It's twenty-nine ninety-nine.

body_content:
Listening: Shopping

In a shop you need to catch numbers fast: prices, sizes and quantities. Read each script aloud and note the key numbers.

1. Script 1: buying clothes

A: Excuse me, how much is this jumper?
B: It's twenty-nine ninety-nine.
A: Have you got it in a medium?
B: Let me check. Yes, in blue or grey.
A: The blue one, please.

Key details: 29.99, medium, blue.

2. Script 2: at the market

A: Two kilos of apples and a bag of oranges, please.
B: That's six fifty.
A: Can I pay by card?
B: Sorry, cash only.

Key details: 2 kilos, 6.50, cash only.

3. Prices and stress

Prices are said in two parts: "twenty-nine ninety-nine" (£29.99). The stress falls on the numbers. Fifteen and fifty sound similar, so listen for the stressed syllable: fifteen / fifty.

4. Useful phrases to recognise

  • Can I help you? a shop assistant starts.
  • Have you got...? / Do you have...? asking for something.
  • Would you like a bag? offering.

5. Where UK and US differ

UKjumper = warm top
trainers = sports shoes
till = where you pay
Have you got...?
USsweater = warm top
sneakers = sports shoes
register or checkout
Do you have...?
Practice tip: when you shop, listen to the price the seller says before you look at the screen.

title: Listening: Voicemail and Announcements

revision.summary: Practise listening to short voicemail messages and public announcements, catching who, when, where and what to do, with UK and US differences.
examples: Hi, it's Mia. Call me back after six.
The next train to Leeds leaves from platform four.

body_content:
Listening: Voicemail and Announcements

Voicemails and announcements are fast and you cannot ask the speaker to repeat. Listen for four things: who, when, where and what to do.

1. Script 1: a voicemail

Hi Tom, it's Mia. I'm calling about Saturday. The party starts at eight, not seven. Can you call me back after six? My number is oh-seven-nine-oh, four-four-one, two-two-six. Thanks, bye!

Who: Mia. When: 8:00, call back after 6. What to do: call back.

2. Script 2: a station announcement

Attention, please. The ten fifteen train to Leeds is delayed by twenty minutes. It will now leave from platform four. We are sorry for the delay.

Key details: train to Leeds, delay of 20 minutes, platform 4.

3. Signal words

not ... but = correction. delayed, cancelled, will now = a change. These words show what to write down first.

4. Where UK and US differ

UKplatform = where the train stops
mobile = phone
Ring me back or call me back
phone: oh, double four
UStrack = where the train stops
cell phone = phone
Call me back
phone: oh, four four
Practice tip: listen to a real voicemail or station announcement and write only the numbers and place names.
